outline.chapter_title: Foundations of Parameter‑Efficient Adaptation for Foundation Models
outline.description: Introduces large foundation models, the need for efficient adaptation, and surveys the main paradigms of parameter‑efficient finetuning.
subtopics: Evolution of foundation models (GPT‑3, Stable Diffusion) and resource constraints
Why full‑model training is prohibitive
Three major PEFT paradigms: model finetuning, adapter modules, prompt tuning
Desiderata for PEFT methods – low parameter budget, no inference latency increase, good generalization

outline.description: Explains the geometric intuition behind preserving relational structure during finetuning and formalizes the OFT framework.
subtopics: Angle preservation between neurons as a principled regularizer
Mathematical formulation: R·W⁰ with R∈ℝ^{d×d} orthogonal
Cayley transform for enforcing orthogonality during training
Zero‑initialization via identity matrix and its effect on stability
Empirical benefits reported in prior OFT work

outline.description: Analyzes why the original OFT suffers from high parameter cost and explores the block‑diagonal compromise.
subtopics: "Dense" versus "block‑diagonal" orthogonal matrices
Parameter scaling O(d²) for full orthogonal matrices
Block‑diagonal OFT: sparsity pattern, reduction to O(b·d) parameters
Inductive bias introduced by fixed block partitioning
Motivation for a dense yet parameter‑efficient orthogonal representation

outline.chapter_title: Information‑Transmission View of Orthogonal Matrix Factorizations
outline.description: Presents a graph‑theoretic perspective that treats matrix factorization as information flow across a grid.
subtopics: Grid representation with d source nodes → d target nodes over m+1 layers
Edges ↔ non‑zero entries in factor matrices B₁,…,B_m
(i) Dense connectivity requirement; (ii) Minimal free edges principle
Implications of orthogonality on edge constraints (full rank = d bijective edges per layer)
Comparison of naive dense factorization versus structured factorizations

outline.description: Introduces butterfly graphs/factorizations from the Cooley–Tukey FFT and shows why they are ideal for efficient information transmission.
subtopics: Recap of radix‑2 Cooley–Tukey algorithm
Definition of butterfly factor B⁽ᴲ⁾(k) and recursive construction of B(d)
Graphical interpretation: O(d log d) edges achieve full connectivity
Historical uses of butterfly matrices in ML (fast linear transforms, RNN stability)
Key properties relevant to orthogonal parameterisation

outline.description: Details the BOFT method – how a product of sparse orthogonal butterfly components yields a dense orthogonal matrix with few parameters.
